title: Gehenna: The Valley Jesus Named
hook: Did Jesus really preach about hell, or about a real valley outside Jerusalem?
tldr: Jesus never said 'hell'; He said Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, infamous for child sacrifice, corpses, refuse and fire. To Jews it meant shame and national judgment, not afterlife torture. Jesus warned Israel as the prophets had, fulfilled when Rome razed Jerusalem in 70 AD. Scripture foresees the valley becoming holy.
big_idea: Gehenna was a real valley of shame, not an eternal torture chamber.

points.title: Gehenna is a real place
points.text: Gehenna comes from Gey Hinnom, a valley southwest of Jerusalem where kings sacrificed children to Molech and Babylon dumped Israel's corpses. It meant shame and disgrace.

points.title: Early readers saw purification
points.text: Origen, who studied with Jews, wrote that Gehenna, where used of the afterlife, meant a place of purification, like the Lord as refiner's fire.

points.title: Undying worms, unquenched fire
points.text: Quoting Isaiah 66:24, Jesus invoked a dump and corpse pit where fires never ceased and worms never lacked food, evoking the Babylonian siege.

points.title: Hyperbole, not self-mutilation
points.text: 'Gouge out your eye' is Jewish hyperbole: evil begins in thought. An outcast adulterer ended up scavenging in Gehenna, the lowest point of shame.

points.title: People shame; God restores
points.text: Hyper-religious society threw sinners into the Valley of Shame. Jesus told the adulterous woman, 'neither do I condemn you.'

points.title: The valley will become holy
points.text: Jeremiah says the valley of dead bodies and ashes will be holy to the LORD, and the Psalmist sees springs there. An eternal hellfire cannot also become holy.

points.title: A warning fulfilled in 70 AD
points.text: Like the prophets, Jesus warned Israel to repent. Forty years later Rome razed Jerusalem; Josephus says over a million died, many corpses thrown into Gehenna.

sections.summary: Calvinist pastor John MacArthur claims Jesus was a hellfire preacher who spoke of hell more than everyone else in the Bible combined. That is incorrect: Jesus never once said 'hell'. He spoke of Gehenna, a well-known Jewish term that first- and second-century Jews understood primarily as harsh consequences, not an afterlife destination.

In Matthew 23:15 Jesus says religious leaders make converts 'twice as much a child of hell' as themselves. Gehenna here is a present reality: moral, spiritual, physical, mental or emotional corruption in this life, a state of separation from God's ways marked by hypocrisy and spiritual blindness, not an eternal place of torment.

Origen, a second-century Church Father who wrote roughly 2,000 treatises and was called the greatest genius of the early church, engaged closely with Jews. In Against Celsus he traced Gehenna to the valley of Ennom in Benjamin's lot, with Jerusalem, and saw it as a place to purify souls, as the Lord comes like a refiner's fire. Even afterlife uses leaned toward temporary correction.

Gehenna comes from Hebrew Gey Hinnom, 'valley of wailing', a real valley southwest of Jerusalem. At Topheth, kings like Ahaz and Manasseh sacrificed children to Molech in fire. The prophets warned enemies would conquer Jerusalem and leaders' corpses would burn there; the fires they lit would consume them. Jeremiah renamed it 'the Valley of Slaughter', where Babylon dumped Israelite corpses.

Israel endured many purifying fires for sin, but child burning was the most abhorrent; Gehenna became synonymous with shame and disgrace. In 1 Enoch, before the New Testament, it symbolized Israel's purifying punishments. God's punishments always purified, or Israel would have ceased to exist, unlike Calvin's or Luther's ideas, which enticed burning and eliminating the Jewish people.

Jesus, also Israel's prophet, used the same images of fire and Gehenna for horrible evils, shame and God's response. God promised not to leave evil unchecked; His justice will consume all evil and remove it from His nation, and He will purify creation once and for all. Gehenna occurs 12 times in the New Testament, translated 'hell' and misread as afterlife torture.

Hinnom lies within today's Kidron Valley national park. Whether it was a garbage dump is hotly debated: Calvinist Francis Chan's 'Erasing Hell' (2011) denied it; DL Kennedy's 'Gehenna Revisited' (2015) rebutted him. A chance excavation found an Early Roman, first-century Jerusalem city dump: household garbage, mostly common tableware and cooking pots, oven fragments, plaster, animal bones and plants, no prestige objects.

Rabbi David Kimhi (1160-1235), on Psalm 27:13, noted fires were kept burning in Hinnom to consume waste and corpses; the Talmud (Erovin 19) links it with fire and smoke. The poor and lepers scavenged there, and with trash always arriving the fires never ceased. Jesus quoted Isaiah: the worm does not die, the fire is not quenched. Worms die, but their food never ran out.

Whether a dump or a corpse site, Hinnom symbolized Israel's disgraceful past and its consequences. Isaiah 66:24 evoked corpses thrown there in the Babylonian siege. Jesus meant a known place of shame and humiliation, warning Israel to repent. Edward William Fudge: a place of undying worm and irresistible fire. Josephus records Romans throwing corpses into the valleys during the siege.

Jesus says lustful looking is adultery of the heart; better to gouge out an eye than be thrown into Gehenna. Having just said He did not come to abolish the Law, would He teach eternal torment for lust, foreign to Moses and Jews? Rabbi Jesus spoke figuratively; a literal reading means advocating self-mutilation. Francis Wright Beare: taken as a demand, it demands the impossible.

His audience likely included children and teenagers. Would He tell them to dismember themselves? Blind people still fantasize. Why would God design sexual impulses and then torture people forever for them? A literal reading misrepresents God and explains religious legalism. Jesus used Jewish hyperbole: evil begins in thought. Lust was one relatable example, addressed by a prophet to a crowd of Jews, the nation.

Someone condemned by society, scavenging leftovers in Gehenna, had hit the lowest point of shame, lost everything, an outcast. So losing an eye beats being thrown into Gehenna's fire. A caught adulterer was stoned or cast out to live in the dump. N.T. Wright: Jesus warned of Gehenna on earth, not burning in the next life. Not every lustful thought leads to adultery, but thoughts become actions.

It was not God who threw people into Hinnom but a hyper-religious society. God wants sinners to live with dignity, be rebuilt and self-sufficient; religious leaders cancel, boycott and degrade them into the Valley of Shame. When religious people brought the woman caught in adultery, Jesus forgave her: 'neither do I condemn you.' Love renews hearts better than the threat of hellfire.

Even the worms show grace in Jewish context. The Talmud (Shabbat 151b) says maggots form for the deceased's benefit, part of God's life-and-death cycle returning dust to dust. Worms recycle nutrients, and larval therapy healed wounds until sulfa ('sulfur or brimstone') drugs took over in the 1940s, then antibiotics. Ancient Israel's view of these metaphors, like fire and brimstone, was more nuanced.

Even if Gehenna were a literal afterlife fire chamber, prophecy contradicts its endlessness. Jeremiah says the whole valley of dead bodies and ashes, out to the Kidron and the Horse Gate, will be holy to the LORD. The Psalmist sees the Valley of Baka (weeping) become a place of springs for pilgrims to Zion. How can endless hellfire become holy and renewed?

In Jewish thought Gehenna meant the severe consequences of straying: nationally, losing God's blessing and protection; individually, sin's outcome in an unforgiving society, left in a wasteland. Like the prophets, Jesus warned: repent or be consumed by Gehenna's flames, scavenging in ashes. Forty years later, in 70 AD, after a five-month siege, Rome razed Jerusalem and the Temple; Josephus counts over a million dead, many thrown into Gehenna.

visuals.title: Matthew 5:27-29 read as hyperbole
visuals.text: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into Gehenna.

mythfact.fact: Jesus never once said 'hell'. He spoke of Gehenna, a real valley that Jews understood as a symbol of harsh consequences and shame.

mythfact.myth: Gehenna is an eternal fire chamber in the afterlife.
mythfact.fact: It was a valley by Jerusalem tied to child sacrifice, corpses and refuse fires, and prophecy says it will become holy to the LORD.

mythfact.myth: Jesus taught that lustful thoughts send you to eternal torment.
mythfact.fact: He used hyperbole: evil starts in thought. An exposed adulterer became an outcast scavenging in Gehenna, the place of shame.

mythfact.fact: A hyper-religious society did that. Jesus refused to condemn the woman caught in adultery.

quotes.text: When Jesus was warning his hearers about Gehenna, he was not, as a general rule, telling them that unless they repented in this life, they would burn in the next one.
Gehenna was a place of undying worm and irresistible fire, an abhorrent place where crawling maggots and smoldering heat raced each other to consume the putrefying fare served them each day.
It was not God who threw individuals into the Valley of Hinnom; it was the people—a hyper-religious society.
